# Zero first-order truncation cost for a fixed nonfacet support direction

This lemma extends the local geometric estimate behind the polytopal contact
argument. It does not provide a finite contact representation for an arbitrary
convex extremizer, and does not bridge the unrestricted and fixed-complexity
extremal classes.

Let K be a convex body in R^d, let n be a unit vector, put h=h_K(n), and let
F=K intersect {n.x=h}. Suppose H_{d-1}(F)=0. For t>=0 sufficiently small put

    K_t=K intersect {n.x<=h-t}.

Then the following statements hold.

1. |K minus K_t|=o(t). Consequently every halfspace-cap volume changes by
   o(t), uniformly over all halfspaces, including moving halfspaces.
2. For every fixed B<infinity, uniformly over |v|<=B and 0<=sigma<=B,

    h_{K_{epsilon sigma}}(n+epsilon v)
      =h+epsilon (h_F(v)-sigma)+o(epsilon).                (1)

   In particular its support improvement over the uncut body is
   epsilon sigma+o(epsilon), uniformly in those parameters.
3. Finitely many such truncations, each in a fixed nonfacet direction and
   each of depth O(epsilon), have total lost volume o(epsilon). Each indexed
   support improvement has the lower bound from (1); the other cuts can only
   improve it further.

## Proof of the volume estimate

In orthogonal coordinates with last coordinate n.x, write A(s) for the
(d-1)-volume of K intersect {n.x=h-s}. These sections stay in one fixed ball.
Every limit point of sections as s decreases to0 lies in F. Hence the
sections eventually lie in every fixed relative neighborhood of F in their
parallel hyperplanes, after translating those hyperplanes to n.x=h.
Since F has zero (d-1)-volume, outer regularity gives A(s)->0. Cavalieri's
formula now gives

    |K minus K_t|=integral_0^t A(s) ds=o(t).

Intersecting the removed set with any measurable cap cannot increase its
volume. This proves the asserted cap-uniform bound without any regularity
of the cap orientation or boundary.

## Proof of the support expansion

Choose q in int(K), and put Delta=h-n.q>0. For x in F and small epsilon,

    y=(1-epsilon sigma/Delta)x+(epsilon sigma/Delta)q

belongs to K_{epsilon sigma}. For an x maximizing v.x on F, evaluation at y
gives, uniformly in the stated parameter ranges,

    h_{K_{epsilon sigma}}(n+epsilon v)
       >=h-epsilon sigma+epsilon h_F(v)-O(epsilon^2).       (2)

For the reverse bound, let x_epsilon be any maximizer in the truncated body.
Boundedness of K and (2) imply

    0<=h-n.x_epsilon<=C epsilon

with one constant C for all allowed v,sigma. Compactness implies

    omega(epsilon)=sup{dist(x,F):x in K, n.x>=h-C epsilon}->0.

The truncation condition and the definition of omega therefore give

    (n+epsilon v).x_epsilon
       <=h-epsilon sigma+epsilon h_F(v)+epsilon B omega(epsilon).

Together with (2), this proves (1). The case sigma=0 is included and gives
the usual one-sided support-function directional derivative. Subtracting
that case from the general case proves the support-improvement statement.
An additional o(epsilon) perturbation of the comparison normal changes each
support value by o(epsilon), by boundedness of K, so the estimate also permits
nearby affine body and target-facet parameters.

For finitely many cuts, the removed set lies in the union of the individually
removed sets, and each individual loss is o(epsilon), uniformly for bounded
nonnegative sigma. Intersecting more cutting halfspaces decreases support
values. This proves statement3.

## What the lemma does not prove

For a polytope target there are only finitely many containment inequalities,
and this lemma can enter the existing finite-dimensional separation argument.
For a general target body, containment involves a continuum of normals.
A stress representation obtained from a finite affine parameter space may
have finitely many atoms, but adding cuts at those atoms changes that
parameter space and can change the stress representation. Thus iteratively
eliminating the currently selected atoms is not a proof that all nonfacet
contact stress vanishes. Uniform convergence of support difference quotients
over every target normal is not asserted by (1): (1) concerns normals within
O(epsilon) of one fixed n.
